title: DaemonSets, StatefulSets & Jobs
summary: Pick the right controller: one Pod per node, Pods with sticky identity, run-to-completion tasks and scheduled tasks.

blocks.text: A DaemonSet makes all (or some) nodes run a copy of a Pod. When a node joins, it gets the Pod; when a node leaves, its Pod is garbage collected. Typical uses: a storage daemon, a log collector or a node monitoring agent on every node. Network plugins often ship a DaemonSet component.

items: `.spec.template` is required; its restart policy must be `Always` (or unset, which defaults to Always).
`.spec.selector` must match the template labels and **can't be changed** after creation.
Set `.spec.template.spec.nodeSelector` or `.spec.template.spec.affinity` to target only some nodes. With neither, Pods go on **all** nodes.
The controller adds a node affinity for the target node to each Pod; the default scheduler then binds it.
If node labels change, Pods are added to newly matching nodes and removed from nodes that no longer match.
Deleting with `--cascade=orphan` leaves the Pods on the nodes. A new DaemonSet with the same selector adopts them.

blocks.text: These tolerations don't cover the control-plane taint. To run daemon Pods on control plane nodes, add a toleration for `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane` (operator `Exists`, effect `NoSchedule`) in the Pod template, as the page's example does.

Like a Deployment, a StatefulSet runs Pods from one template, but the Pods are **not interchangeable**. Each keeps its identity across rescheduling. Use it when you need stable network IDs, stable persistent storage, or ordered deployment, scaling and rolling updates.

items: **Ordinal:** with N replicas, Pods get ordinals 0 to N-1 (or from `.spec.ordinals.start`). The label `apps.kubernetes.io/pod-index` holds it.
**Name/hostname:** `<statefulset-name>-<ordinal>`, e.g. a StatefulSet `web` gives `web-0`, `web-1`, `web-2`.
**DNS:** you must create a **headless Service** (`clusterIP: None`) and name it in `serviceName`. Each Pod gets `<pod-name>.<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`.
**Storage:** each `volumeClaimTemplates` entry gives every Pod its own PVC. If no StorageClass is named, the default one is used.
Scaling down or deleting a StatefulSet does **not** delete its volumes by default (`persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` defaults to `Retain`).

blocks.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  serviceName: <headless-service>
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: <label>
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: <label>
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: <container>
        image: <image>
        volumeMounts:
        - name: <claim-name>
          mountPath: <path>
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: <claim-name>
    spec:
      accessModes: [ "ReadWriteOnce" ]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: <size>

items: With the default `podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady`, Pods are created in order 0 → N-1, each waiting for the previous one to be Running and Ready.
Pods are terminated in reverse order, N-1 → 0, and a Pod is only removed once all higher ordinals have fully shut down.
`podManagementPolicy: Parallel` launches or terminates all Pods at once, without waiting.
Deleting a StatefulSet gives no ordering guarantee. Scale it to 0 first if you need a graceful, ordered shutdown.

rows: Replaces Pods one at a time from the highest ordinal down. `rollingUpdate.partition` updates only ordinals ≥ the partition
No automatic update; new Pods use the new template only after you delete the old ones

blocks.text: StatefulSets keep revisions too (as ControllerRevisions, default `revisionHistoryLimit` 10): `kubectl rollout history statefulset/<name>` and `kubectl rollout undo statefulset/<name> --to-revision=<n>`.
If a bad template never becomes Ready under OrderedReady, reverting the template isn't enough. You must also delete the Pods that already tried the bad config.
A Job creates Pods and keeps retrying until a set number of them **succeed**. If a Pod fails or its node dies, the Job starts a new one, so prefer a Job over a bare Pod even for a single task.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  completions: <n>      # successful Pods needed
  parallelism: <n>      # Pods running at once
  backoffLimit: 4       # retries before the Job fails
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: <container>
        image: <image>
        command: [<cmd>]
      restartPolicy: Never   # Never or OnFailure only

rows: Leave completions and parallelism unset (both default to 1)
Set completions; parallelism defaults to 1. `completionMode: Indexed` gives each Pod an index 0 to completions-1

items: `.spec.template` is the only required field. Don't set `.spec.selector` in almost all cases.
`parallelism: 0` effectively pauses the Job. `.spec.suspend: true` suspends it and terminates its running Pods.
`kubectl logs jobs/<name>` shows the output; `kubectl delete jobs/<name>` deletes the Job and its Pods.

rows: Retries before the Job is marked failed
Max run time for the whole Job; then Pods are killed, reason `DeadlineExceeded`. Wins over backoffLimit
Delete the finished Job (and its Pods) this many seconds later; 0 = right away

items: Failed Pods are recreated with an exponential back-off (10s, 20s, 40s …) capped at six minutes.
With `restartPolicy: OnFailure` the container restarts in the same Pod; with `Never` the whole Pod fails and a new one is created.
Terminal conditions: `Complete` on success, `Failed` on failure. A failed Job is **not** restarted automatically.
Finished Jobs and their Pods stay around (so you can read logs) until you delete them or a TTL or CronJob history limit removes them.

blocks.text: Both the Job spec and the Pod spec have an `activeDeadlineSeconds` field. Set it at the Job level to cap the Job.
A CronJob creates a Job on a repeating schedule, like one line of a crontab. `.spec.schedule` and `.spec.jobTemplate` are required.

# minute  hour  day-of-month  month  day-of-week(0-6, Sun=0)
0 3 * * 1     # Mondays at 03:00
*/2           # step value: every 2 (e.g. in the hour field)
@hourly = 0 * * * *    @daily = 0 0 * * *    @weekly = 0 0 * * 0

rows: `Allow` (default), `Forbid` (skip the new run if the last is still going), `Replace` (replace the running Job)
Skip a run that can't start within this many seconds of its scheduled time
`true` stops future runs (default false); already-started Jobs keep going
Finished Jobs to keep: defaults 3 and 1
e.g. `Etc/UTC`. Unset = kube-controller-manager's local time. CRON_TZ/TZ in the schedule is rejected

items: Editing a CronJob only affects Jobs created afterwards.
Scheduling is approximate: occasionally two Jobs, or none, may be created, so make Jobs **idempotent**.
CronJob names may be at most 52 characters, because the controller appends 11 characters and Job names max out at 63.

questions.stem: You need a log collector running on every node, including nodes added later. Which controller fits?

options.explanation: A DaemonSet adds the Pod to each node as it joins.

options.text: Deployment with replicas equal to the node count
options.explanation: A Deployment doesn't control which host each Pod lands on, or follow node changes.
StatefulSets give sticky identity, not one Pod per node.
CronJobs run Jobs on a schedule.

questions.stem: Which tolerations does the DaemonSet controller add to its Pods automatically? Select 3.

options.explanation: So daemon Pods aren't evicted from not-ready nodes.
That's why daemon Pods can run on nodes marked unschedulable.
Listed among the automatic tolerations.
Not automatic; the page's example adds it in the Pod template.

questions.stem: True or false: You can change a DaemonSet's `.spec.selector` after it has been created.

options.explanation: The selector can't be mutated once the DaemonSet exists.
Changing it could orphan Pods, so it's immutable.

questions.stem: A database needs each replica to keep its own volume and a stable hostname after rescheduling. Which controller should you use?

options.explanation: Each Pod gets a sticky identity and its own PVC.
Deployment Pods are interchangeable and have no stable identity.
That runs one Pod per node, not stable per-replica storage.
Jobs are for tasks that run to completion.

questions.stem: StatefulSet `web` has 3 replicas and the default Pod management policy. You scale it to 1. What happens?

options.text: web-2 is terminated first; web-1 only after web-2 has fully shut down
options.explanation: Termination runs in reverse ordinal order, one at a time.

options.text: web-0 and web-1 are terminated together
options.explanation: The lowest ordinal is kept; Pods go from the highest down.
StatefulSets remove Pods in a defined order.

options.text: All Pods are recreated with new names
options.explanation: Remaining Pods keep their identity.

questions.stem: You scale a StatefulSet from 5 to 2 replicas. What happens to the PVCs of the removed Pods by default?

options.explanation: The default retention policy is Retain, for data safety.

options.text: They are deleted with the Pods
options.explanation: Only if whenScaled is set to Delete.

options.text: They are attached to the remaining Pods
options.explanation: Each PVC belongs to one Pod identity.

questions.stem: A StatefulSet has 5 replicas and `rollingUpdate.partition: 3`. You change the image. Which Pods are updated?

options.explanation: Only Pods with an ordinal greater than or equal to the partition are updated.
Those are below the partition and stay on the old version.
The partition holds back the lower ordinals.
That's the OnDelete strategy.

questions.stem: Which `restartPolicy` is NOT allowed in a Job's Pod template?

options.explanation: Jobs only allow Never or OnFailure.
Never is allowed.
OnFailure is allowed.

questions.stem: You need 10 successful runs of a task, with at most 3 Pods at a time. Which Job settings do that?

options.explanation: completions counts successes; parallelism caps concurrent Pods.
That's reversed.
backoffLimit counts retries, not successes.
That's a work-queue Job with 10 Pods at once.

questions.stem: A Job has `backoffLimit: 5` and `activeDeadlineSeconds: 100`. Its Pods keep failing, and 100 seconds pass after only 2 retries. What happens?

options.text: The Job fails with reason DeadlineExceeded and its running Pods are terminated
options.explanation: activeDeadlineSeconds takes precedence over backoffLimit.
The deadline stops new Pods even if backoffLimit isn't reached.
A failed Job isn't restarted automatically.
No Pod succeeded, so it can't be Complete.

questions.stem: Which statements about finished Jobs are correct? Select 2.

options.text: Completed Pods are kept by default so you can read their logs
options.explanation: Pods usually aren't deleted when the Job completes.

options.text: ttlSecondsAfterFinished lets the TTL controller delete the Job and its Pods
options.explanation: The TTL controller deletes the Job cascadingly.

options.text: Finished Jobs are deleted immediately by default
options.explanation: Without a TTL, the Job stays until you delete it.

options.text: Deleting a Job with kubectl leaves its Pods running
options.explanation: kubectl delete removes the Job's Pods too.

questions.stem: A CronJob's backup sometimes runs longer than its interval. You never want two backups at once; a late run should be skipped. Which setting fits?

options.explanation: Forbid skips the new run while the previous one is still going.
Replace stops the running Job and starts the new one.
Allow (the default) lets runs overlap.
That stops all future runs.

questions.stem: True or false: Editing a CronJob's job template also updates Jobs that are already running.

options.explanation: Changes only apply to Jobs created after the edit.
Running Jobs and their Pods continue unchanged.

questions.stem: Which CronJob schedule runs once a day at midnight?

options.explanation: Equivalent to @daily.
That's @hourly.
That's @weekly (Sunday).
That's @monthly.

questions.stem: A StatefulSet rollout to a bad image is stuck under OrderedReady. You revert the template, but nothing changes. What else must you do?

options.text: Delete the Pods that were already started with the bad configuration
options.explanation: The StatefulSet keeps waiting for the broken Pod; deleting it lets the reverted template take effect.
That only keeps more ControllerRevisions; it doesn't unstick the rollout.
That only breaks network identity.

options.text: Wait; it recovers on its own
